description: We are a team of four technology enthusiasts from Karachi, Pakistan. Naveed (FAST-NUCES, BS AI) specializes in AI, ML, and Agentic AI. Hussain (NED, BE SE) focuses on Full-Stack Development. Rafey (KU, BE SE) specializes in Data Science, while Taha (KU, BS CS) excels in 3D Modeling and Design. We aim to combine our skills to build innovative, impactful solutions addressing challenges related to space, Earth, and humanity.
summary:
Zero-G Ember is a web dashboard, built by Team QuadraNova, that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into clear, source-linked fire-safety answers for crewed habitats and a future Moon base.

What we developed: We processed 24 NASA investigations from the Physical Sciences Informatics archive into 1,998 test records and 10,533 searchable report passages. The dashboard ranks investigations for fire prevention, detection and suppression, using weights you can change. It plots every real test on an oxygen-and-pressure flammability map, with a Moon-base mode (at least 30% oxygen, at most 10.2 psi). It also has a cited AI analyst, where code rejects any uncited or invented claim.

How it meets the challenge: It summarizes, ranks and interprets the research, and it shows the gaps: only 48 Moon-air tests with outcomes, and no partial-gravity tests.

Why it matters: Fire is a critical risk in space, and the evidence is scattered across about 13.4 TB. This tool makes it usable, traceable and honest about what is unknown.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Zero-G Ember is a web dashboard over 24 NASA microgravity combustion investigations. It turns the archive into 1,998 test rows and 10,533 searchable report passages. It has a flammability map (every test plotted by oxygen and pressure, with a Moon-base mode), a ranking of investigations for fire prevention, detection and suppression, a gaps view, and a cited AI analyst.

The AI works in five steps: you ask a question, we search the passages and test rows, code does the counting, the model writes using only labelled evidence ([E1], [E2]...), and code rejects any uncited sentence or fake source before you see it.

What benefits does it have?

  • Turns about 13.4 TB of scattered research into answers a person can read in seconds.
  • Every statement traces back to a NASA file and row.
  • It states what the data does not cover (48 Moon-air tests, no partial-gravity tests) instead of guessing.
  • The ranking weights are visible and adjustable.
  • The map, ranking and 20 research FAQs keep working even if the AI is unavailable.

What is the intended impact?

To help researchers, mission planners and students find fire-safety evidence quickly for spacecraft and Moon habitats, and to show where new experiments are needed, especially tests at lunar gravity. The Earth benefits page also links the research to cleaner engines, burners and fire models. It supports decisions and does not make them.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript and Python 3.12.
  • Web: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, and hand-written SVG charts, deployed on Vercel.
  • Data pipeline: Python standard library plus pypdf, reading NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) API and public files.
  • Search and AI: BM25 retrieval written by us; Google Gemini free tier (primary) and Groq (backup); our own citation checker.
  • Other: GitHub, headless Edge for testing and screenshots, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.
  • Hardware: an ordinary Windows laptop. No GPU or special equipment.

How is your project creative?

  • A checkable AI: the model sees only labelled evidence and code verifies every citation, so it can't invent a source.
  • Moon Base Mode: it isolates the tests that match planned habitat air (at least 30% oxygen, at most 10.2 psi).
  • A map of every real test, with gray dots for unrecorded outcomes instead of guessed ones.
  • A transparent ranking with a prevention, detection and suppression lens and changeable weights.
  • A gaps view that makes the missing data part of the result.
  • Design: a space and Moon theme with dark and light modes and smooth scroll animation.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Trust: we wrote 15 test questions before running the AI, and fixed the checker, not the questions, when it failed. We state that the checker proves a citation exists, not full reasoning.
  • Honesty: only about a third of rows have outcome labels, and all Moon-air tests come from one experiment in microgravity, not on the Moon.
  • Cost and limits: free AI quotas are small, so 21 checked answers are pre-generated and live Ask is a bonus.
  • Data size: we never downloaded the raw video archive and kept to curated tables and reports.
  • Safety: downloaded files were treated as untrusted.
  • Accessibility: a colour-blind-safe palette, reduced-motion support and a phone layout.
  • Not official: this is an independent tool built on NASA's public data, not a NASA product.
